doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Hearing a 1967 Rainbow Room recording with Joe Williams
summary: Monk Rowe plays an unreleased tape of Mabern with Joe Williams; he recalls Duke Ellington and Jimmy Jones visiting and praises Hugh Walker.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: Well I want to play something for you. I noticed the last couple of days you’ve got quite a musical memory for some of the things you’ve done. I tried to fool you or see if you could recognize something you did with Lee Morgan, and you got it right up. But this particular thing I don’t think you’ll —
[audio interlude]
First of all, does it sound like somebody you know?
Sounds very — I think you got me this time. It sounds very familiar. It almost sounds like me but —
It is you.
But I’m trying to —
It’s not something that was ever on a record.
That’s what I’m wondering about. Yeah. What is that? Oh that’s Joe Williams. That’s Joe. Yeah. I knew it sounded like me but I didn’t recognize it. I said I didn’t recall recording that on a record.
Well this is you and Joe in about 1967 from the Rainbow Room.
The Rainbow Room.
In New York City.
In New York City.
And the reason I have this is because Joe apparently had someone record it.
Right.
And Jillean gave us all these tapes. And so this is like —

Isn’t that something, the Rainbow Room. We were probably up there for maybe sometimes we’d be up there maybe three or four or five weeks at a time. And Duke Ellington would come by because Joe loved Duke, you know. Duke loved to sing with

the maestro and I’d tell him go ahead and play something, he’d play. Jimmy Jones would come by. Because Joe loved Jimmy Jones. And he’d always tell me, he would say, you know, not necessarily play like Jimmy Jones but listen. Which I had no problem with that because Jimmy Jones and Jerome Richardson were the ones that recommended me for the job with Joe Williams, you know. But yeah, isn’t that something. I think one time we played up there and Big Nick was the guest, and Joe Newman.
That’s — he’s on this recording.
Isn’t that something. I knew it sounded like me but I didn’t recall recording anything record-wise, that’s why I had to listen to it yeah.
Yeah. Well I’d love to find a record company who would be willing to put something like that out.
That sure would be good for sure, yeah.
You know I think Hugh Walker played on it.
Hugh Walker, yeah, rest his soul.
So that’s pretty neat that you’re here.

Hugh Walker is one of those kind of drummers like he carried his own rhythm. He had his rhythm in his hip pocket. I mean the minute he sat down. He was on one of my favorite record dates “Rakin’ and Scrapin’.” Hugh Walker is on that. Hugh Walker, George Coleman, Blue Mitchell and Bill Lee. Yeah, Hugh Walker.
